warmup.q: The ledger pool has 8 threads (core and max), a bounded queue of 80 slots and a policy that throws. Each transfer takes 5 ms. 300 transfers arrive within a few milliseconds. About how many are accepted?
options: About 80: the size of the queue
warmup.why: From Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection: the 8 core threads take the first 8 tasks, the next 80 fill the queue, and with core equal to max the pool can't grow, so the other 212 go to the rejection policy. The demo in this lesson accepts exactly 88, because submitting 300 tasks takes less time than the first 5 ms transfer.

sections.h: Every pool setting is a decision
sections.html:
Lesson 1's ledger is correct on any number of threads. Now it needs threads to run on. In production a transfer does more than change two numbers. It first appends to a journal, a write-ahead log on disk, so a crash can't lose a transfer that a caller was told was accepted. Say that write takes 5 ms. The ledger needs a pool for that work, and the default pools are each wrong in their own way. Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) has an unbounded queue, so a slow disk turns into millions of queued transfers and an out-of-memory error. Executors.newCachedThreadPool() has no thread limit, so the same slow disk turns into thousands of threads.

Build the pool yourself and write down a reason for each setting:

Java
PoolPlan plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(1_600, Duration.ofMillis(5), Duration.ofMillis(50));   // 8 and 80
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        plan.threads(), plan.threads(),                    // core == max: no burst threads
        0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(plan.queueCapacity()),    // bounded: a full queue pushes back
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(),  // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... in every dump
        new CountingAbortPolicy());                        // counted, then thrown at the caller
pool.prestartAllCoreThreads();
Kotlin
val plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(1_600, Duration.ofMillis(5), Duration.ofMillis(50))      // 8 and 80
val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(
    plan.threads(), plan.threads(),                        // core == max: no burst threads
    0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
    ArrayBlockingQueue(plan.queueCapacity()),              // bounded: a full queue pushes back
    Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(),      // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... in every dump
    CountingAbortPolicy())                                 // counted, then thrown at the caller
pool.prestartAllCoreThreads()

The sizes come from Little's law, from Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law: in flight = arrival rate x time in the system. At a peak of 1,600 transfers a second, each holding a thread for 5 ms, 1,600 x 0.005 = 8 transfers are in flight, so 8 threads. With fewer, the queue grows at every peak. With many more, you only add threads that wait on the same disk.

The queue gets the same law. A busy pool finishes 1,600 transfers a second, so 80 queued transfers drain in 80 / 1,600 = 50 ms. If 50 ms is the longest a transfer should wait for a thread, 80 slots is the most the queue should hold. A queue of 10,000 would hide six seconds of waiting behind a client's timeout.

Core equals max because extra threads would only add waiters on the same journal, and the pool grows past core only when the queue is full. Here, the right answer to a full queue is no.

That makes the rejection policy the last decision. DiscardPolicy and DiscardOldestPolicy drop a transfer, so they are never right for money. CallerRunsPolicy makes the submitting thread write the journal itself: fine for a batch importer, wrong for an HTTP thread with a client waiting. For the API path, count and throw. The handler answers 503 with Retry-After, the client retries with the same transfer id, and the counter shows on the dashboard.

try.title: Send a burst at the pool
steps: Run BurstDemo: 300 transfers of 5 ms each arrive at once at the pool above. Predict how many are accepted and how long submitting takes.
Run it with -Pargs=callerRuns. Predict how many transfers the submitting thread runs itself, and how long submitting takes now.

code.title: BurstDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionHandler; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * A burst of 300 transfers hits a pool sized with Little's law: 8 threads, 80 queue slots, 5 ms * per transfer. Pass "callerRuns" to swap the counting abort policy for CallerRunsPolicy. */ public class BurstDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean callerRuns = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("callerRuns"); AtomicInteger rejected = new AtomicInteger(); RejectedExecutionHandler policy = callerRuns ? new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // the submitting thread runs it itself : (task, pool) -> { // count it, then throw at the caller rejected.incrementAndGet(); throw new RejectedExecutionException("ledger pool full"); }; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(80), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), policy); pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); AtomicInteger ranOnCaller = new AtomicInteger(); String caller = Thread.currentThread().getName(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); int accepted = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) { try { pool.execute(() -> { if (Thread.currentThread().getName().equals(caller)) ranOnCaller.incrementAndGet(); sleep(5); // the journal write }); accepted++; } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { // an HTTP handler would answer 503 with Retry-After here } } long submitMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long doneMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%s: accepted %d, rejected %d, run by the submitting thread %d%n", callerRuns ? "CallerRunsPolicy" : "counting abort", accepted, rejected.get(), ranOnCaller.get()); System.out.printf("submitting took %d ms, all done after %d ms%n", submitMs, doneMs); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

Pass "callerRuns" to swap the counting abort policy for CallerRunsPolicy. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val callerRuns = args.firstOrNull() == "callerRuns" val rejected = AtomicInteger() val policy: RejectedExecutionHandler = if (callerRuns) ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // the submitting thread runs it itself else RejectedExecutionHandler { _, _ -> // count it, then throw at the caller rejected.incrementAndGet() throw RejectedExecutionException("ledger pool full") } val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(80), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), policy) pool.prestartAllCoreThreads() val ranOnCaller = AtomicInteger() val caller = Thread.currentThread().name val t0 = System.nanoTime() var accepted = 0 repeat(300) { try { pool.execute { if (Thread.currentThread().name == caller) ranOnCaller.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(5) // the journal write } accepted++ } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { // an HTTP handler would answer 503 with Retry-After here } } val submitMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS) val doneMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("%s: accepted %d, rejected %d, run by the submitting thread %d" .format(if (callerRuns) "CallerRunsPolicy" else "counting abort", accepted, rejected.get(), ranOnCaller.get())) println("submitting took $submitMs ms, all done after $doneMs ms") }

try.expect: With the counting abort policy, 88 are accepted (8 running, 80 queued) and 212 are rejected within a few milliseconds; the accepted ones are done after roughly 60 to 120 ms (88 x 5 ms / 8 threads, plus start-up). With CallerRunsPolicy nothing is rejected, but the submitting thread ran 24 transfers itself and submitting took about 130 ms instead of 4. While it writes a journal entry it can't submit, which is the back-pressure. If that thread were serving an HTTP request, its client would have waited all that time for other people's transfers.

sections.h: Shut down by draining, and account for every transfer
sections.html:
A deploy stops the ledger while transfers are queued, and each of them belongs to a caller who was told "accepted". So the rule for shutdown is this: when it ends, every accepted transfer has been applied, has failed with an error its caller saw, or has been handed back to you by id. None may vanish.

pool.shutdownNow() on its own breaks that rule. It interrupts the running tasks and returns the queued ones as a List<Runnable>. Ignore the list and those transfers are gone. Worse, their futures never complete, so a caller blocked in get() waits forever. In this section's demo a bare shutdownNow() loses 992 of 1,000 transfers.

The order from Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown fixes it:

Java
public ShutdownReport shutdown(Duration grace) throws InterruptedException {
    pool.shutdown();                                              // 1. no new transfers; the queue drains
    if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS))
        return new ShutdownReport(true, List.of());               // 2. everything accepted was applied
    List<Transfer> neverStarted = new ArrayList<>();
    for (Runnable r : pool.shutdownNow()) {                       // 3. interrupt, take back the queue
        TransferTask task = (TransferTask) r;
        task.cancel(false);                                       //    wakes a caller blocked in get()
        neverStarted.add(task.transfer());
    }
    pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
    return new ShutdownReport(false, List.copyOf(neverStarted));  // 4. log them, or replay them
}
Kotlin
fun shutdown(grace: Duration): ShutdownReport {
    pool.shutdown()                                               // 1. no new transfers; the queue drains
    if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS))
        return ShutdownReport(true, emptyList())                  // 2. everything accepted was applied
    val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow().map { r ->              // 3. interrupt, take back the queue
        val task = r as TransferTask
        task.cancel(false)                                        //    wakes a caller blocked in get()
        task.transfer
    }
    pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
    return ShutdownReport(false, neverStarted)                    // 4. log them, or replay them
}

Two details make this work. First, the queue must hold objects that know their transfer. pool.submit(callable) wraps your work in an anonymous FutureTask, so the lab's submit builds a TransferTask, a FutureTask subclass with a transfer() accessor, and hands it to execute. Then shutdownNow() gives you back transfers instead of mystery Runnables.

Second, an interrupted task must leave nothing half-done. Each task writes the journal first and changes memory second. An interrupt during the write means the transfer was never applied: its future fails with the InterruptedException, and no balance changed. apply itself never blocks, so once it starts, it finishes.

Size the grace period from the same numbers as the pool. A full queue of 80 drains in 50 ms, so a few seconds of grace fits easily inside the 30 seconds Kubernetes gives a pod by default.

try.title: Lose transfers, then stop losing them
steps: Run ShutdownDemo -Pargs=naive: 1,000 accepted transfers, then a bare shutdownNow(). Read the lost column and the last line.
Run it with no arguments (drain, 100 ms of grace), then with -Pargs='drain 5000'. Before each run, predict how many transfers are applied.

code.title: ShutdownDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.FutureTask; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * 1,000 transfers wait on 8 threads at 5 ms each, then the service stops. Where does each one end up? * Args: "naive" or "drain" (the default), then the grace period in ms (default 100). */ public class ShutdownDemo { record Transfer(int id) {} // a FutureTask that remembers its transfer, so the queue hands back transfers, not anonymous Runnables static final class TransferTask extends FutureTask<Boolean> { final Transfer transfer; TransferTask(Transfer transfer, Callable<Boolean> work) { super(work); this.transfer = transfer; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "drain"; long graceMs = args.length > 1 ? Long.parseLong(args[1]) : 100; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()); AtomicInteger applied = new AtomicInteger(), interrupted = new AtomicInteger(); List<TransferTask> accepted = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) { TransferTask task = new TransferTask(new Transfer(i), () -> { try { Thread.sleep(5); // the journal write } catch (InterruptedException e) { interrupted.incrementAndGet(); // not journaled, so not applied throw e; } applied.incrementAndGet(); return true; }); pool.execute(task); accepted.add(task); } int handedBack = 0; if (mode.equals("naive")) { pool.shutdownNow(); // the list of queued tasks it returns is dropped } else { pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new work; the queue keeps draining if (!pool.awaitTermination(graceMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // 2. interrupt, take back the queue for (Runnable r : neverStarted) ((TransferTask) r).cancel(false); // 3. wake anyone waiting on them handedBack = neverStarted.size(); // 4. log these ids, or replay them on restart } } pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long neverComplete = accepted.stream().filter(t -> !t.isDone()).count(); System.out.printf("%s, grace %d ms: accepted 1,000 | applied %,d | interrupted %d | handed back %,d | lost %,d%n", mode, graceMs, applied.get(), interrupted.get(), handedBack, 1_000 - applied.get() - interrupted.get() - handedBack); System.out.printf("futures that will never complete: %,d%n", neverComplete); } }

Where does each one end up? * Args: "naive" or "drain" (the default), then the grace period in ms (default 100). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.getOrElse(0) { "drain" } val graceMs = args.getOrNull(1)?.toLong() ?: 100 val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(1_000), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()) val applied = AtomicInteger() val interrupted = AtomicInteger() val accepted = (0 until 1_000).map { i -> QueuedTask(QueuedTransfer(i)) { try { Thread.sleep(5) // the journal write } catch (e: InterruptedException) { interrupted.incrementAndGet() // not journaled, so not applied throw e } applied.incrementAndGet() true }.also { pool.execute(it) } } var handedBack = 0 if (mode == "naive") { pool.shutdownNow() // the list of queued tasks it returns is dropped } else { pool.shutdown() // 1. no new work; the queue keeps draining if (!pool.awaitTermination(graceMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() // 2. interrupt, take back the queue neverStarted.forEach { (it as QueuedTask).cancel(false) } // 3. wake anyone waiting on them handedBack = neverStarted.size // 4. log these ids, or replay them on restart } } pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) val neverComplete = accepted.count { !it.isDone } println("%s, grace %d ms: accepted 1,000 | applied %,d | interrupted %d | handed back %,d | lost %,d".format( mode, graceMs, applied.get(), interrupted.get(), handedBack, 1_000 - applied.get() - interrupted.get() - handedBack)) println("futures that will never complete: %,d".format(neverComplete)) }

try.expect: Naive: about 990 lost, and as many futures that will never complete, so their callers would hang. Drain with 100 ms: about 160 applied (8 threads x 20 rounds of 5 ms), 8 interrupted in the middle of their journal write, the rest handed back, and 0 lost. With 5 s of grace all 1,000 are applied, because they need only about 625 ms on 8 threads.

refs.title: ExecutorService (Java SE 25 API): the shutdown idiom

sections.h: Publish a snapshot nobody can tear
sections.html:
The balances endpoint wants every balance at once, and invariant 1 says they must add up to the opening total. Reading the accounts one at a time, each under its own lock, doesn't give you that:

Java
long sum = 0;
for (Account a : accounts) {
    a.lock().lock();
    try { sum += a.balance(); } finally { a.lock().unlock(); }   // each read is safe...
}                                                                  // ...the sum is not
Kotlin
var sum = 0L
for (a in accounts) {
    sum += a.lock.withLock { a.balance }                         // each read is safe...
}                                                                  // ...the sum is not

A transfer from account 40 to account 3 can run after you read 3 and before you read 40. Then you counted that money in neither account. In the other direction you count it twice. In the demo, a large share of such sums were wrong, by up to 13,957 cents, although no transfer ever broke an invariant. A sum like that is torn: it mixes two moments.

A consistent snapshot needs one instant at which no transfer is half done. Lock every account, in the same id order that apply uses so the snapshot can't deadlock with a transfer, copy the balances, then release:

Java
public BalanceSnapshot snapshot() {
    for (Account a : inLockOrder) a.lock().lock();                 // 1. every lock, in id order
    try {
        Map<String, Long> copy = new HashMap<>();
        long total = 0;
        for (Account a : inLockOrder) { copy.put(a.id(), a.balance()); total += a.balance(); }
        BalanceSnapshot s = new BalanceSnapshot(copy, total, ++version);   // 2. immutable
        latest = s;                                                // 3. volatile write: published whole
        return s;
    } finally {
        for (int i = inLockOrder.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) inLockOrder.get(i).lock().unlock();
    }
}
Kotlin
fun snapshot(): BalanceSnapshot {
    inLockOrder.forEach { it.lock.lock() }                         // 1. every lock, in id order
    try {
        val copy = inLockOrder.associate { it.id to it.balance }
        val s = BalanceSnapshot(copy, copy.values.sum(), ++version) // 2. immutable
        latest = s                                                 // 3. @Volatile write: published whole
        return s
    } finally {
        inLockOrder.asReversed().forEach { it.lock.unlock() }
    }
}

For 50 accounts this pauses transfers for microseconds, and readers call latestSnapshot() without taking any lock. Happens-before, the rules that matter asked you to name the edge for every shared field. Here they are:

Field Why every reader sees it correctly
Account.balance the account's lock: each release happens-before the next acquire
accounts, inLockOrder final fields, set in the constructor, never changed
version written only while every account lock is held
latest volatile: its write happens-before every later read
a snapshot's balances and total final fields of a record, holding a map that Map.copyOf made unmodifiable
a Transfer in the pool immutable, and execute happens-before the task runs
a transfer's outcome the task's completion happens-before Future.get() returns

Writing latest before the locks are released keeps snapshots in version order: two snapshots can't overlap, because each needs every lock.

try.title: Tear a snapshot, then make it whole
steps: Run TornSnapshotDemo. Four threads move money while the main thread adds up all 50 balances, one locked account at a time. Predict how many sums come out wrong.
Run it with -Pargs=locked, where the reader holds every lock while it adds.

code.title: TornSnapshotDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * Four threads move money between 50 accounts while a reader adds up all the balances. * Pass "locked" to make the reader hold every account lock while it adds. */ public class TornSnapshotDemo { static final class Account { final int id; final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); long balance = 1_000; // guarded by lock: 50,000 in total Account(int id) { this.id = id; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean locked = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("locked"); Account[] accounts = new Account[50]; for (int i = 0; i < accounts.length; i++) accounts[i] = new Account(i); AtomicBoolean writing = new AtomicBoolean(true); List<Thread> writers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int w = 0; w < 4; w++) { writers.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current(); for (int n = 0; n < 200_000; n++) { int a = rnd.nextInt(50), b = rnd.nextInt(49); if (b >= a) b++; move(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(500)); } })); } long taken = 0, torn = 0, worst = 0; while (writers.stream().anyMatch(Thread::isAlive)) { long sum = locked ? sumAllLocked(accounts) : sumOneByOne(accounts); taken++; if (sum != 50_000) { torn++; worst = Math.max(worst, Math.abs(sum - 50_000)); } } System.out.printf("%s: %,d snapshots, %,d torn (worst off by %,d cents)%n", locked ? "every lock held" : "one account at a time", taken, torn, worst); } // each read is safe on its own; the sum is not, because money moves between reads static long sumOneByOne(Account[] accounts) { long sum = 0; for (Account a : accounts) { a.lock.lock(); try { sum += a.balance; } finally { a.lock.unlock(); } } return sum; } // every lock, in id order: no transfer can run while we add, so the sum is one instant static long sumAllLocked(Account[] accounts) { for (Account a : accounts) a.lock.lock(); try { long sum = 0; for (Account a : accounts) sum += a.balance; return sum; } finally { for (int i = accounts.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) accounts[i].lock.unlock(); } } static void move(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id < to.id ? from : to, second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock.lock(); try { second.lock.lock(); try { if (from.balance >= cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents; } } finally { second.lock.unlock(); } } finally { first.lock.unlock(); } } }

alt.title: TornSnapshotDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.withLock private class SnapshotAccount(val id: Int) { val lock = ReentrantLock() var balance = 1_000L // guarded by lock: 50,000 in total } /** * Four threads move money between 50 accounts while a reader adds up all the balances. * Pass "locked" to make the reader hold every account lock while it adds. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val locked = args.firstOrNull() == "locked" val accounts = Array(50) { SnapshotAccount(it) } val writers = List(4) { Thread.ofPlatform().start { val rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current() repeat(200_000) { val a = rnd.nextInt(50) var b = rnd.nextInt(49) if (b >= a) b++ move(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(500)) } } } var taken = 0L var torn = 0L var worst = 0L while (writers.any { it.isAlive }) { val sum = if (locked) sumAllLocked(accounts) else sumOneByOne(accounts) taken++ if (sum != 50_000L) { torn++ worst = maxOf(worst, Math.abs(sum - 50_000)) } } println("%s: %,d snapshots, %,d torn (worst off by %,d cents)" .format(if (locked) "every lock held" else "one account at a time", taken, torn, worst)) } // each read is safe on its own; the sum is not, because money moves between reads private fun sumOneByOne(accounts: Array<SnapshotAccount>): Long = accounts.sumOf { a -> a.lock.withLock { a.balance } } // every lock, in id order: no transfer can run while we add, so the sum is one instant private fun sumAllLocked(accounts: Array<SnapshotAccount>): Long { accounts.forEach { it.lock.lock() } try { return accounts.sumOf { it.balance } } finally { accounts.reversed().forEach { it.lock.unlock() } } } private fun move(from: SnapshotAccount, to: SnapshotAccount, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to val second = if (first === from) to else from first.lock.withLock { second.lock.withLock { if (from.balance >= cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents } } } }

try.expect: One account at a time, many sums are wrong (7,241 of 9,456 in one Java run here, 1,226 of 6,239 in a Kotlin run), some by thousands of cents, while every transfer kept the books balanced. With every lock held, no sum is torn. A real service wouldn't let every request take all the locks: it takes one snapshot every few hundred milliseconds and lets readers share it through latestSnapshot().

sections.h: Find a hung pool in a thread dump
sections.html:
Here is a bug that passes every test with a small batch. A month-end statement job runs on the ledger pool, and each statement asks the same pool for a balance:

Java
pool.submit(() -> {
    Future<Long> balance = pool.submit(() -> balanceOf(merchant));   // a task inside a task
    return merchant + ": " + balance.get();                          // waits for it
});
Kotlin
pool.submit(Callable {
    val balance = pool.submit(Callable { balanceOf(merchant) })      // a task inside a task
    "$merchant: ${balance.get()}"                                    // waits for it
})

With 2 threads and 3 merchants, the first two statements take both threads. Each submits a balance lookup, which queues behind the third statement. Now both threads wait for tasks that need a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown called this pool-induced deadlock. This section is about finding it in a running process.

Start PoolHangDemo with a long hang, then dump its threads from a second terminal:

jcmd                          # lists Java processes and their PIDs
jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l    # -l adds the java.util.concurrent locks each thread holds

Here is the part that matters, from a real run on JDK 21, trimmed:

"ledger-0" #19 [5741] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=1.33ms elapsed=1.74s ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method)
	- parking to wait for  <0x00000006f79ef530> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)
	at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/LockSupport.java:221)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.awaitDone(java.base@21.0.12.1/FutureTask.java:500)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(java.base@21.0.12.1/FutureTask.java:190)
	at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.statement(PoolHangDemo.java:33)
	at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.lambda$main$0(PoolHangDemo.java:21)
	...
	at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(java.base@21.0.12.1/ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1144)
	...
   Locked ownable synchronizers:
	- <0x00000006f79650b8> (a java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker)

"ledger-1" #20 [5742] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.83ms elapsed=1.74s ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method)
	- parking to wait for  <0x00000006f7602c18> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)
	...
	at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.statement(PoolHangDemo.java:33)
	...
   Locked ownable synchronizers:
	- <0x00000006f79bb838> (a java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker)

Read each thread in the same order. The name says which pool: both ledger- threads are stuck, which is why the factory names them. The state, WAITING (parking), means java.util.concurrent parked them; a thread stuck on synchronized would say BLOCKED. The parking to wait for line names the object they wait on: a FutureTask, so they are inside get(). The first frame from your own code, statement at line 33, is that get() call. And under Locked ownable synchronizers each worker holds its own ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker, a lock a worker holds while it runs a task. Both threads are busy, and busy waiting.

Notice what is missing: the dump never says Found one Java-level deadlock. The JVM's detector looks for cycles of monitors and ReentrantLocks, and here nobody holds a lock that anybody else wants. Every worker of one pool parked on a FutureTask of that same pool, with tasks still queued, is the signature to learn. The fixes come from that lesson: do the lookup inline, compose with thenApply instead of blocking, or give lookups their own pool.

try.title: Take the dump yourself
steps: Run PoolHangDemo with -Pargs=60 so it stays hung for a minute. It prints its PID.

In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l. For both ledger- threads, find the state, the parking to wait for line, the first frame from workbench.ledger, and the Locked ownable synchronizers. Then find main.
Scroll to the end of the dump. Is there a deadlock report? Explain why not.
Change statement to call balanceOf(merchant) directly instead of submitting it, and run the demo again.

code.title: PoolHangDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * Month-end statements on the ledger pool: each statement task asks the same 2-thread pool for a * balance and waits for the answer. Run it, then take a thread dump while it hangs. * Arg: how many seconds to stay hung (default 4). */ public class PoolHangDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int seconds = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()); for (String merchant : List.of("m-001", "m-002", "m-003")) { pool.submit(() -> statement(pool, merchant)); } long pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid(); System.out.printf("pid %d, hanging for %d s. In another terminal: jcmd %d Thread.print -l%n", pid, seconds, pid); Thread.sleep(seconds * 1_000L); System.out.printf("after %d s: active=%d, queued=%d, completed=%d%n", seconds, pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size(), pool.getCompletedTaskCount()); pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the two get() calls that will never return } static String statement(ExecutorService pool, String merchant) throws Exception { Future<Long> balance = pool.submit(() -> balanceOf(merchant)); // queued behind the other statements return merchant + ": " + balance.get(); // waits for a thread that is never free } static long balanceOf(String merchant) { return 4_200; // fast: the problem is not speed } }

alt.title: PoolHangDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.ledger.l02.demo import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * Month-end statements on the ledger pool: each statement task asks the same 2-thread pool for a * balance and waits for the answer. Run it, then take a thread dump while it hangs. * Arg: how many seconds to stay hung (default 4). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val seconds = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 4 val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(100), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()) for (merchant in listOf("m-001", "m-002", "m-003")) { pool.submit(Callable { statement(pool, merchant) }) } val pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid() println("pid $pid, hanging for $seconds s. In another terminal: jcmd $pid Thread.print -l") Thread.sleep(seconds * 1_000L) println("after $seconds s: active=${pool.activeCount}, queued=${pool.queue.size}, completed=${pool.completedTaskCount}") pool.shutdownNow() // interrupts the two get() calls that will never return } private fun statement(pool: ExecutorService, merchant: String): String { val balance = pool.submit(Callable { balanceOf(merchant) }) // queued behind the other statements return "$merchant: ${balance.get()}" // waits for a thread that is never free } private fun balanceOf(merchant: String): Long = 4_200 // fast: the problem is not speed

try.expect: Both ledger-0 and ledger-1 are WAITING (parking) on a FutureTask inside PoolHangDemo.statement, each holding its ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker, and main is TIMED_WAITING (sleeping) in Thread.sleep. There is no deadlock report, because no thread holds a lock another thread wants. When the sleep ends the demo prints active=2, queued=3, completed=0: the third statement and both lookups never ran. With the lookup inline, it prints completed=3. The Kotlin twin shows the same dump with PoolHangDemoKt.statement as your frame.

analogy: A pool is a bank branch with eight tellers and a waiting area with eighty chairs. When every chair is taken, the guard at the door tells the next customer to come back in a minute and makes a tally mark (the counting rejection). Hiring a teller for every customer, or letting the queue spill out into the street, only looks kind. At closing time the guard locks the door, the tellers finish the people already seated, and anyone still waiting at the deadline gets a numbered ticket for tomorrow instead of being sent home with nothing. The analogy breaks at the statement job: a real teller who needs a colleague's help walks over and asks. A pool thread that waits for a task in its own queue just stands at its desk, and so do all the others.
world: Quarkus runs blocking endpoints on a worker pool whose size you set with quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads, and the argument for that number is this lesson's: in flight = rate x time, with the time measured under load. When Kubernetes stops a pod it sends SIGTERM and waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 by default), so fail the readiness probe first, drain the ledger pool within a deadline inside that window, and log the ids of any transfer handed back so someone can replay it. A Temporal worker's limit on concurrent activities is a pool size too: size it from the activity's rate and duration in the same way, and watch for activities that block waiting on work that needs the same slots.
mistake: The most common mistake is an unbounded queue: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n), or a LinkedBlockingQueue with no capacity. Nothing is ever rejected, so tests and dashboards look healthy while a slow disk or database grows the queue by thousands of transfers a second. Latency climbs to minutes, clients time out and retry, which adds more work, and the pod finally dies of memory with its queue full of transfers that callers were told were accepted. People choose it because it is the default and because rejecting feels worse than waiting. Bound the queue from Little's law, and turn the overflow into a counted, visible rejection.

compare.title: Starting the pool and submitting a transfer

java.title: LedgerService.java
java.html: public static LedgerService start(Ledger ledger, Journal journal, PoolPlan plan) { CountingAbortPolicy rejections = new CountingAbortPolicy(); ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads(), plan.threads(), 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(plan.queueCapacity()), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), rejections); pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); return new LedgerService(ledger, journal, pool, rejections); } public Future<Outcome> submit(Transfer t) { TransferTask task = new TransferTask(t, () -> { journal.append(t); return ledger.apply(t); }); pool.execute(task); return task; } static final class TransferTask extends FutureTask<Outcome> { private final Transfer transfer; TransferTask(Transfer transfer, Callable<Outcome> work) { super(work); this.transfer = transfer; } Transfer transfer() { return transfer; } }

kotlin.title: LedgerService.kt
kotlin.html: fun start(ledger: Ledger, journal: Journal, plan: PoolPlan): LedgerService { val rejections = CountingAbortPolicy() val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads, plan.threads, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(plan.queueCapacity), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), rejections) pool.prestartAllCoreThreads() return LedgerService(ledger, journal, pool, rejections) } fun submit(t: Transfer): Future<Outcome> { val task = TransferTask(t) { journal.append(t) ledger.apply(t) } pool.execute(task) return task } class TransferTask(val transfer: Transfer, work: Callable<Outcome>) : FutureTask<Outcome>(work)

compare.note: Nothing here is specific to either language: ThreadPoolExecutor, ArrayBlockingQueue and Thread.ofPlatform() are the same JDK classes, with the same rules. Kotlin shortens the FutureTask subclass to one line, because the constructor parameter work goes straight to the superclass in the class header, and a trailing lambda converts to the Java Callable. When you call pool.submit with a bare lambda, Kotlin has to choose between submit(Runnable) and submit(Callable); writing Callable { ... } says which you mean. In coroutine code, Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(8) caps parallelism like this pool, but it queues without a bound and never rejects, so it can't replace the back-pressure.

worked.title: Size the pool for a new peak

steps.say: The sales forecast for a promotion day is 4,000 transfers a second. Under load the journal's write takes 4 ms. You want no transfer to wait more than 100 ms for a thread. Start with Little's law, for both halves of the pool.
steps.code: // 1. peak rate, time each transfer holds a thread, longest acceptable queue wait PoolPlan plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(4_000, Duration.ofMillis(4), Duration.ofMillis(100)); // 2. 4,000/s x 0.004 s = 16 in flight; 4,000/s x 0.1 s = 400 waiting System.out.println(plan); // PoolPlan[threads=16, queueCapacity=400]

alt.html: // 1. peak rate, time each transfer holds a thread, longest acceptable queue wait val plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(4_000, Duration.ofMillis(4), Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 2. 4,000/s x 0.004 s = 16 in flight; 4,000/s x 0.1 s = 400 waiting println(plan) // PoolPlan[threads=16, queueCapacity=400]

steps.say: Now check the downstream, as Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law insisted. The storage team says the journal volume handles 12 concurrent writes before each one slows down. With 16 threads, the extra 4 just queue inside the journal and make every write slower. The real ceiling is the journal's: 12 writes / 0.004 s = 3,000 transfers a second, whatever the forecast says.

Size from the scarce resource, and let the rejection policy handle the rest. At 3,000 a second, 100 ms of queue is 300 slots. Above that rate the pool rejects and counts, and the API answers 503 with Retry-After.
steps.code: // 3. the journal takes 12 writes at once: that sets the threads, and the throughput PoolPlan capped = new PoolPlan(12, 300); // 12 / 0.004 s = 3,000 a second; 3,000 x 0.1 s = 300 slots LedgerService service = LedgerService.start(ledger, journal, capped);

alt.html: // 3. the journal takes 12 writes at once: that sets the threads, and the throughput val capped = PoolPlan(12, 300) // 12 / 0.004 s = 3,000 a second; 3,000 x 0.1 s = 300 slots val service = LedgerService.start(ledger, journal, capped)

steps.say: If 3,000 isn't enough, more threads won't help, because the journal is the bottleneck. Make each write do more: group commit (one disk flush for a batch of transfers) raises what 12 concurrent writes can carry. Then check shutdown again: 300 queued transfers on 12 threads at 4 ms drain in 100 ms, so a 5 s grace period still fits well inside Kubernetes' 30 s.

lab.title: Put the ledger on a pool, drain it, and publish snapshots
steps: Run the tests once. All eight fail. Ledger.apply is already lesson 1's solution. Read the field comments at the top of Ledger: they name the happens-before edge for every field.
Write PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw: Math.ceilDiv(perSecond * d.toNanos(), 1_000_000_000L) for both numbers, and never less than 1.

Write LedgerService.start (the pool from section 1), submit (a TransferTask that appends to the journal and then applies, passed to pool.execute) and CountingAbortPolicy.rejectedExecution (count, then throw).
Write LedgerService.shutdown in the order from section 2: shutdown, awaitTermination, then shutdownNow, cancel and collect each TransferTask, wait once more, and report.
Write Ledger.snapshot: lock every account in inLockOrder, copy the balances, build the snapshot with ++version, write latest, and release in reverse order in a finally.
Run the tests until all eight pass, then twice more.
hints: Use pool.execute(task), not pool.submit(task). submit would wrap your TransferTask in another FutureTask, and shutdownNow() would hand back that wrapper.
The shutdown test's journal blocks until it is interrupted. If your shutdown hangs, check that you call shutdownNow() when the first awaitTermination returns false.
If the torn-snapshot test fails, check that you take every lock before you read any balance, and release none until the snapshot is built and published.
perSecond * timePerTransfer.toNanos() multiplies an int by a long, so Java computes it as a long. It doesn't overflow at these sizes.
lab.done: All eight tests in LedgerServiceTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the drain-then-hand-back shutdown from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write List<Runnable> stop(ExecutorService pool, Duration grace): stop taking new work, let the queue drain for at most grace, then interrupt what is still running and return the tasks that never started, after cancelling any of them that are futures. If you are interrupted while waiting, keep the interrupt flag set.

answer.html: List<Runnable> stop(ExecutorService pool, Duration grace) { pool.shutdown(); // no new work; the queue keeps draining try { if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) return List.of(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the flag, then stop hard } List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the running tasks for (Runnable r : neverStarted) { if (r instanceof Future<?> f) f.cancel(false); // a caller blocked in get() wakes up } return neverStarted; // log them, or replay them }

alt.html: fun stop(pool: ExecutorService, grace: Duration): List<Runnable> { pool.shutdown() // no new work; the queue keeps draining try { if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) return emptyList() } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // keep the flag, then stop hard } val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() // interrupts the running tasks neverStarted.forEach { (it as? Future<*>)?.cancel(false) } // a caller blocked in get() wakes up return neverStarted // log them, or replay them }

recap: Size a pool with Little's law: threads = peak rate x time per task, queue = peak rate x the longest wait you accept. Then check the downstream's own limit, which may be lower.
Bound the queue, set core equal to max, name the threads, and choose the rejection policy on purpose: for money on the API path, count and throw, never discard.
Shut down in order: shutdown, awaitTermination with a deadline, then shutdownNow; cancel what it returns and log or replay those transfers. None may vanish.
Journal first, apply second, and never block inside apply. Then an interrupt can only stop a transfer that hasn't changed anything yet.
A sum of separately locked reads is torn. A consistent snapshot holds every lock in the global order, copies, and publishes an immutable record through a volatile field.
A pool hung on its own tasks shows every named worker WAITING (parking) on a FutureTask in get(), each holding its Worker lock, and no deadlock report.

explain.prompt: An on-call engineer asks why the ledger pool has only 8 threads and 80 queue slots when the machine has memory for thousands. Explain where both numbers come from, and what happens when traffic goes above the plan.
explain.answer: Both come from Little's law. At the planned peak of 1,600 transfers a second, each transfer holds a thread for about 5 ms while the journal writes it, so 1,600 x 0.005 = 8 transfers are in flight. Eight threads keep up, and more would only wait on the same journal. The queue absorbs bursts, but every queued transfer waits: a busy pool finishes 1,600 a second, so 80 queued transfers wait at most 50 ms, the longest wait we accept. A bigger queue would hide seconds of latency until clients time out and retry. Above the plan the queue fills, and the counting policy rejects the extra transfers at once: the API answers 503 with Retry-After, the client retries with the same transfer id, and the rejection counter shows the overload. If that happens often, we measure the journal again and resize, or make each journal write cheaper.

deeper.html:
Locking every account costs time in proportion to the number of accounts, and it stops every writer while it copies. At 50 accounts that is microseconds. At five million accounts it is a pause your clients feel. Three designs avoid it.

Snapshot per shard. Split the accounts into shards, route every transfer to one shard, and snapshot each shard on its own. The grand total is the sum of the shard totals, which is only consistent while no transfer crosses a shard.

Copy-on-write state. Keep all balances in an immutable map behind an AtomicReference, and make every transfer a compare-and-set of a new map. Readers get a consistent snapshot for free with get(). Writers pay for the copy and retry when another writer won, so this fits read-heavy books with modest write rates. It is the snapshot idea from Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal, used for writes too:

Java
private final AtomicReference<Map<String, Long>> balances =
        new AtomicReference<>(Map.of("alice", 100L, "bob", 0L));

boolean transfer(String from, String to, long cents) {
    while (true) {
        Map<String, Long> now = balances.get();                   // a consistent snapshot, for free
        if (now.get(from) < cents) return false;
        Map<String, Long> next = new HashMap<>(now);              // copy, change two entries
        next.merge(from, -cents, Long::sum);
        next.merge(to, cents, Long::sum);
        if (balances.compareAndSet(now, Map.copyOf(next))) return true;   // retry if another writer won
    }
}
Kotlin
private val balances = AtomicReference(mapOf("alice" to 100L, "bob" to 0L))

fun transfer(from: String, to: String, cents: Long): Boolean {
    while (true) {
        val now = balances.get()                                  // a consistent snapshot, for free
        if (now.getValue(from) < cents) return false
        val next = now + mapOf(from to now.getValue(from) - cents, to to now.getValue(to) + cents)
        if (balances.compareAndSet(now, next)) return true        // retry if another writer won
    }
}

Event sourcing. Treat the journal as the truth and a snapshot as the result of applying it up to a position. You can build snapshots on a replica that reads the journal, and the live ledger never stops for them.

For dumps, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json <file> writes the same information as JSON, which tools can group and count. Lesson 3 of this track uses it on 10,000 virtual threads.
